d.g: An atrophic type of chronic non-specific rhinitis characterized by a foul odor from the nose, now considered rare.
Any of the beetles in genus Ozaena, with one species, Ozaena dentipes.
an area of low mountains in northwestern Arkansas and southeastern Missouri and northeastern Oklahoma
United States conductor (born in Japan in 1935)
a chronic disease of the nose characterized by a foul-smelling nasal discharge and atrophy of nasal structures
A dark waxy mineral, found associated with petroleum in some sandstones, used to make polishes.
Alternative form of ozocerite.
An allotrope of oxygen (symbol O₃) having three atoms in the molecule instead of the usual two; it is a toxic gas, generated from oxygen by electrical discharge.
d.x: Lightning flashed again, the thunder came a second later. It rained harder. The smell of ozone was strong. You could feel the charge in the air.

d.g: Fresh air, especially that breathed at the seaside and smelling of seaweed.
d.x: To Ramsgate baths she sped, in quest / Of seaweed and ozone ; / For seaweed and ozone were best, / They said, to give her tone.

d.g: To treat with ozone.
d.x: I worked nonstop to make the house safe. Periodically I ozoned the first-floor bathroom, but it still made us sick.

ozone.e: From German Ozon, coined 1840 by Christian Friedrich Schönbein, from Ancient Greek ὄζον (ózon), neuter participle of ὄζω (ózō, “I smell”), in reference to its pungent odour. The “fresh air” sense is from an erroneous former belief that seaweed contains and releases ozone.

d.g: the univalent anion, O₃⁻, derived from ozone
any dark red salt of this anion and a metal
any of a number of explosive organic compounds containing a -O-O-O- group

any of a class of heterocycles, containing two carbon atoms (in positions 3 and 5) and three oxygen atoms (in positions 1, 2 and 4) produced by the reaction of ozone with a carbon to carbon double bond; the 1,2,4-trioxolanes

ozonide.e: English ozone Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Italic *-iðos Latin -idusder. English -ide English ozonide From ozone + -ide.

d.g: A carpet of hyphae, resembling an above-ground mycelium, associated with certain mushrooms of the genus Coprinellus.
A layer in part of the stratosphere that has a larger than normal concentration of ozone; the ozone layer.

ozonosphere.e: English ozone Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der. Latin -o-bor. English -o- Ancient Greek σφαῖρᾰ (sphaîră)bor. Latin sphaera Late Latin sphērader. Old French spherebor. Middle English spere English sphere English -sphere English ozonosphere From ozone + -o- + -sphere.

d.g: genus of Australian shrubs and perennial herbs;  sometimes included in genus Helichrysum
Alternative spelling of ozonize.
d.x: There isn't a silly fad that she hasn't taken up—and what's more tragic, absolutely believed in for the time—from ozonised milk to rhythmic yawning.

ozonise.e: English ozone English -ise English ozonise From ozone + -ise.

d.g: To treat or react with ozone; to ozonate
To convert oxygen into ozone, especially by using an ozonizer

ozonize.e: English ozone Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English ozonize From ozone + -ize.
